description: Hand-curated plain-language content for the techniques that realistically surface as top gaps: the union of technique_priorities.json (all tiers) and threat_profiles.json (industry + actor profiles). Each entry: 'definition' (one sentence a non-technical reader understands), 'attacker_use' (completes the sentence 'Attackers use this to …'), 'detection_hint' (vendor-neutral sketch of what a good detection watches for — feeds the 'what would good look like' block and the Phase 14c XLSX). Written once, reviewed like code — never generated at runtime. ID validity and coverage of the curated rule are test-enforced (test_mitre_plain_language.py). Long-tail techniques fall back to the first sentence of the ATT&CK description in attack.json.

T0831.definition: Interfering with an industrial control process so it no longer behaves the way operators intend.
T0831.attacker_use: disrupt or damage physical operations such as production lines, power delivery, or safety systems.
T0831.detection_hint: unexpected setpoint or control-command changes on OT controllers outside maintenance windows

T0883.definition: An industrial device (PLC, HMI, controller) that is reachable directly from the internet.
T0883.attacker_use: reach the OT network directly without first breaching the corporate IT network.
T0883.detection_hint: inbound connections to OT devices from public internet addresses; OT protocol traffic crossing the IT/OT boundary

T0886.definition: Using legitimate remote-access services (VNC, RDP, SSH) to reach systems inside the industrial network.
T0886.attacker_use: move around OT networks with trusted admin tools instead of malware.
T0886.detection_hint: new or unusual remote sessions to engineering workstations or HMIs, especially from outside the OT subnet

T1003.001.definition: Reading the memory of the Windows LSASS process, where the passwords and hashes of recently logged-on users live.
T1003.001.attacker_use: steal the credentials of everyone who recently signed in to a machine and reuse them elsewhere.
T1003.001.detection_hint: non-system processes opening a handle to lsass.exe; credential-dumping tools such as mimikatz or procdump targeting LSASS

T1003.003.definition: Copying the Active Directory database file (NTDS.dit), which holds password hashes for every account in the domain.
T1003.003.attacker_use: obtain every domain credential at once — a common step right before ransomware deployment.
T1003.003.detection_hint: volume shadow copy creation on domain controllers followed by access to NTDS.dit; ntdsutil or vssadmin runs on domain controllers

T1021.001.definition: Logging in to another computer's desktop over Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP).
T1021.001.attacker_use: move from machine to machine hands-on-keyboard using stolen credentials.
T1021.001.detection_hint: RDP logons from unusual source machines or at odd hours, and by accounts that do not normally use RDP

T1021.002.definition: Connecting to hidden Windows administrative shares (C$, ADMIN$) to copy files or run programs on other machines.
T1021.002.attacker_use: push tools and ransomware to many machines quickly.
T1021.002.detection_hint: admin-share connections from ordinary workstations rather than admin hosts; remote service creation right after an SMB logon

T1021.004.definition: Logging in to other systems over SSH with valid or stolen credentials and keys.
T1021.004.attacker_use: move between Linux servers and network devices while looking like an administrator.
T1021.004.detection_hint: SSH logins from new source hosts, or accounts connecting to servers outside their normal set

T1027.definition: Disguising malicious files, scripts, or commands — encoding, encrypting, or packing them so scanners and humans cannot read them.
T1027.attacker_use: slip payloads past antivirus and reviewers.
T1027.detection_hint: command lines containing base64 or other encoded payloads; scripts with unusually high entropy or nested encoding

T1036.definition: Making a malicious file or process look legitimate — for example a fake 'svchost.exe' running from the wrong folder.
T1036.attacker_use: hide in plain sight among normal system activity.
T1036.detection_hint: well-known system process names running from non-standard paths; files whose extension does not match their content

T1041.definition: Sending stolen data out through the same channel the malware already uses for remote control.
T1041.attacker_use: steal data without opening any new, more visible connection.
T1041.detection_hint: unusually large or sustained outbound transfers on existing beaconing connections

T1046.definition: Scanning the network to find which systems and services are reachable.
T1046.attacker_use: map out targets to spread to next.
T1046.detection_hint: one host connecting to many hosts or ports in a short window; scan patterns from machines that are not vulnerability scanners

T1047.definition: Using Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) — a built-in administration framework — to run commands, often on remote machines.
T1047.attacker_use: execute payloads remotely without dropping obvious tools.
T1047.detection_hint: wmic or WmiPrvSE spawning unexpected child processes; WMI process creation on remote hosts

T1053.005.definition: Creating a Windows scheduled task that runs a payload automatically.
T1053.005.attacker_use: persist across reboots and run code at times of their choosing.
T1053.005.detection_hint: scheduled-task creation by unusual processes; new tasks pointing at user-writable or temporary paths

T1055.definition: Injecting code into another running process so the payload executes inside a trusted program.
T1055.attacker_use: hide malware inside legitimate processes and inherit their permissions.
T1055.detection_hint: processes writing into other processes' memory (remote-thread and similar API sequences); unexpected modules loaded into system processes

T1059.001.definition: Running commands or scripts through PowerShell, the scripting engine built into every Windows machine.
T1059.001.attacker_use: download and execute payloads with a tool that is always present and often trusted.
T1059.001.detection_hint: encoded (-enc) or download-cradle PowerShell command lines; PowerShell launched by Office applications or other unusual parents

T1059.003.definition: Running commands through the Windows command shell (cmd.exe).
T1059.003.attacker_use: chain built-in Windows commands for execution and reconnaissance.
T1059.003.detection_hint: cmd.exe with long, chained, or obfuscated one-liner command lines, especially when spawned by documents or server processes

T1059.007.definition: Running malicious JavaScript outside the browser, typically via the Windows script hosts (wscript/cscript).
T1059.007.attacker_use: execute droppers delivered as .js email attachments or downloads.
T1059.007.detection_hint: wscript or cscript executing .js files from mail, download, or temp folders

T1071.001.definition: Hiding command-and-control traffic inside normal-looking web (HTTP/HTTPS) traffic.
T1071.001.attacker_use: blend their remote-control channel in with everyday web browsing.
T1071.001.detection_hint: regular fixed-interval beacons to rare domains; web traffic with abnormal header patterns or payload sizes

T1078.definition: Logging in with real, stolen credentials instead of using malware.
T1078.attacker_use: look exactly like a legitimate user while gaining and keeping access.
T1078.detection_hint: logons at unusual times or from unusual locations and hosts; dormant accounts suddenly becoming active

T1078.004.definition: Signing in to cloud services (Microsoft 365, AWS, Google) with stolen cloud credentials.
T1078.004.attacker_use: reach email and cloud data directly — no malware on any machine.
T1078.004.detection_hint: cloud sign-ins showing impossible travel, anonymizing proxies, or unfamiliar devices

T1082.definition: Collecting basic details about a machine — operating system, hostname, hardware, and patch level.
T1082.attacker_use: size up each machine before choosing their next step.
T1082.detection_hint: bursts of recon commands such as systeminfo and hostname, especially run by scripts or service accounts

T1087.002.definition: Listing the user accounts that exist in the Windows domain.
T1087.002.attacker_use: find admin and service accounts worth stealing.
T1087.002.detection_hint: net user /domain, nltest, or LDAP enumeration bursts from ordinary workstations

T1098.definition: Changing an existing account — resetting its password, or adding permissions or group memberships.
T1098.attacker_use: expand or preserve access using accounts defenders already trust.
T1098.detection_hint: unexpected password resets, group-membership additions, or permission grants, especially on privileged accounts

T1098.001.definition: Adding extra credentials — API keys, certificates, or app secrets — to a compromised cloud account or application.
T1098.001.attacker_use: keep cloud access even after the original password is reset.
T1098.001.detection_hint: new API keys, application secrets, or certificates added to accounts or service principals outside change windows

T1059.005.definition: Running Visual Basic code — often VBA macros embedded in Office documents — to execute attacker instructions.
T1059.005.attacker_use: get code running the moment a victim opens a malicious document.
T1059.005.detection_hint: Office applications spawning child processes; documents with macros making network connections shortly after opening

T1071.004.definition: Hiding command-and-control traffic inside ordinary-looking DNS queries and responses.
T1071.004.attacker_use: communicate with compromised machines through a channel that is rarely blocked or inspected.
T1071.004.detection_hint: unusually long or high-volume DNS queries to a single domain; DNS requests with encoded-looking subdomains

T1091.definition: Spreading malware by copying it onto USB drives or other removable media that later gets plugged into another machine.
T1091.attacker_use: cross into networks that have no direct internet or network connection.
T1091.detection_hint: autorun-style execution immediately after a removable drive is connected; unexpected executables appearing on USB media

T1105.definition: Downloading additional attacker tools onto a machine that is already compromised.
T1105.attacker_use: bring in stronger tooling after the first foothold.
T1105.detection_hint: certutil, bitsadmin, or curl downloading executables; binaries fetched from rare external hosts by non-installer processes

T1113.definition: Taking screenshots of a victim's screen without their knowledge.
T1113.attacker_use: see what the victim is doing, including sensitive data displayed on screen.
T1113.detection_hint: processes calling screen-capture APIs on a schedule, especially from tools with no legitimate reason to do so

T1114.002.definition: Reading a victim's email directly from a cloud mailbox (e.g. Exchange Online, Gmail) using stolen credentials or tokens.
T1114.002.attacker_use: search a mailbox for sensitive information or hijack ongoing email threads for fraud.
T1114.002.detection_hint: mailbox access or mail-forwarding-rule changes from unusual locations or applications, especially via API/legacy-auth protocols

T1189.definition: Compromising a legitimate website so that simply visiting it infects the victim's browser.
T1189.attacker_use: infect targeted visitors without sending them anything directly — a 'watering hole' attack.
T1189.detection_hint: browser or plugin crashes/exploitation followed by new process creation; unexpected outbound connections right after visiting a specific site

T1199.definition: Abusing a trusted third party — an MSP, vendor, or contractor with legitimate access — to reach the real target.
T1199.attacker_use: reach a well-defended target through a less-defended partner that already has access.
T1199.detection_hint: third-party/vendor accounts or connections behaving outside their normal scope of access

T1110.definition: Guessing account passwords by trying many candidates.
T1110.attacker_use: break into accounts without any prior credential theft.
T1110.detection_hint: many failed logons in a short window against one or more accounts, followed by a success

T1110.003.definition: Trying one common password (like 'Summer2026!') against many accounts, staying under lockout limits.
T1110.003.attacker_use: find the one account using a weak seasonal password without triggering account lockouts.
T1110.003.detection_hint: the same source failing logons across many different accounts within a short period

T1110.004.definition: Trying username/password pairs leaked from breaches of other websites.
T1110.004.attacker_use: exploit people reusing the same password for personal and work accounts.
T1110.004.detection_hint: logon attempts across many accounts with one failure each, often from cloud or anonymized IP pools

T1112.definition: Changing Windows registry keys to alter system behavior or hide configuration.
T1112.attacker_use: persist, weaken defenses, or stash payload data inside the registry.
T1112.detection_hint: registry changes to run keys, security settings, or service configuration made by unusual processes

T1133.definition: Logging in from the internet through the organization's own remote-access services — VPN, Citrix, or exposed RDP.
T1133.attacker_use: walk in through the front door with stolen credentials.
T1133.detection_hint: VPN or remote-gateway logons from unusual countries, without the expected MFA, or from new devices

T1136.001.definition: Creating a new local user account on a compromised machine.
T1136.001.attacker_use: keep a way back in that survives password resets of the stolen account.
T1136.001.detection_hint: account-creation events outside normal provisioning, especially on servers

T1190.definition: Exploiting a vulnerability in an internet-facing application or appliance — a web app, VPN gateway, or mail server.
T1190.attacker_use: gain a first foothold without phishing anyone.
T1190.detection_hint: exploit-pattern requests and error spikes on public applications; web-server processes spawning shells or unexpected children

T1195.002.definition: Tampering with software you legitimately install — a poisoned update or compromised vendor package.
T1195.002.attacker_use: ride trusted software straight into many organizations at once.
T1195.002.detection_hint: software updates connecting to unexpected hosts or spawning unusual processes right after installation

T1203.definition: Exploiting a vulnerability in a client application — browser, Office, or PDF reader — when a user opens content.
T1203.attacker_use: turn opening a document or web page into code execution.
T1203.detection_hint: office, reader, or browser processes crashing and then spawning shells or script engines

T1204.002.definition: Tricking a user into opening a malicious file attachment or download.
T1204.002.attacker_use: have the victim run the payload themselves.
T1204.002.detection_hint: documents spawning script engines or shells (for example winword starting powershell); executables launched from mail or temp folders

T1218.011.definition: Abusing rundll32.exe — a signed Windows utility — to execute malicious code under a trusted name.
T1218.011.attacker_use: run payloads under a Microsoft-signed binary that security tools often ignore.
T1218.011.detection_hint: rundll32 running with no arguments, odd DLL paths or exports, or making network connections

T1219.definition: Installing legitimate remote-administration software — AnyDesk, TeamViewer, ScreenConnect — as a backdoor.
T1219.attacker_use: keep remote control through commercial software many companies allow.
T1219.detection_hint: remote-access tools installed on machines with no business need; connections to unapproved remote-tool services

T1482.definition: Mapping the trust relationships between Windows domains.
T1482.attacker_use: find paths from a small foothold domain into the main corporate domain.
T1482.detection_hint: nltest /domain_trusts or trust-enumeration LDAP queries from non-admin hosts

T1485.definition: Deleting or overwriting data to make it unrecoverable.
T1485.attacker_use: destroy evidence or cause damage — sometimes destruction is the whole goal.
T1485.detection_hint: mass file deletions or overwrites in a short window; wiper-style tools; bulk deletions in cloud storage

T1486.definition: Encrypting files across your systems and demanding payment — the final act of a ransomware attack.
T1486.attacker_use: hold data and operations hostage for ransom.
T1486.detection_hint: rapid mass file modification and renames with new extensions; ransom-note files; shadow-copy deletion just before

T1489.definition: Stopping a running service or process, including security tools and backup agents.
T1489.attacker_use: disable defenses or disrupt operations before the main attack, or as the disruption itself.
T1489.detection_hint: unexpected service-stop events for security/backup services; sc stop or net stop commands outside maintenance windows

T1490.definition: Deleting backups, shadow copies, and recovery features before doing damage.
T1490.attacker_use: make sure you cannot simply restore instead of paying.
T1490.detection_hint: vssadmin delete shadows, wbadmin delete catalog, or bcdedit recovery changes — near-certain ransomware precursors

T1499.definition: Overwhelming a system or service with traffic or requests so legitimate users cannot use it.
T1499.attacker_use: disrupt operations directly, or as a distraction/extortion lever alongside another attack.
T1499.detection_hint: sudden abnormal spikes in inbound traffic or request volume against a specific service; service unavailability without a deployment change

T1505.003.definition: Planting a small script (web shell) on a web server that gives command execution through an ordinary browser.
T1505.003.attacker_use: keep durable access to a compromised server hidden behind normal web traffic.
T1505.003.detection_hint: web-server processes spawning shells; new or modified script files appearing in web directories

T1528.definition: Stealing OAuth access tokens that grant applications access to cloud accounts, including via consent phishing.
T1528.attacker_use: read cloud mail and files without ever touching the password — MFA does not stop an already-granted token.
T1528.detection_hint: unusual OAuth application consents, especially requesting mail or file permissions; token use from new infrastructure

T1543.003.definition: Installing or modifying a Windows service to run attacker code.
T1543.003.attacker_use: persist with SYSTEM-level privileges across reboots.
T1543.003.detection_hint: new service installations pointing at unusual or user-writable paths

T1547.001.definition: Adding a program to the registry Run keys or the Startup folder so it launches at every logon.
T1547.001.attacker_use: survive reboots with a decades-old trick that still works.
T1547.001.detection_hint: new run-key values or startup-folder files pointing at temp or user-writable paths

T1552.001.definition: Finding passwords stored in files — scripts, configuration files, spreadsheets, or a 'passwords.txt'.
T1552.001.attacker_use: harvest credentials nobody realized were written down.
T1552.001.detection_hint: searches for 'password' across file shares; bulk reads of configuration files by user accounts

T1557.definition: Getting between two systems on the network to capture or alter their traffic (adversary-in-the-middle).
T1557.attacker_use: capture credentials and relay authentication on the local network.
T1557.detection_hint: LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning responses, rogue ARP announcements, or unexpected NTLM relay patterns

T1560.001.definition: Compressing collected data with archive tools (7-Zip, WinRAR, tar) before stealing it.
T1560.001.attacker_use: package loot into fewer, smaller, often password-protected transfers.
T1560.001.detection_hint: archive utilities run on servers or unusual hosts; password-protected archives written to staging or temp folders

T1566.001.definition: A targeted email carrying a malicious attachment.
T1566.001.attacker_use: get an initial foothold by having one person open one file.
T1566.001.detection_hint: mail with executable or macro attachments from new senders; attachment opens followed by script-engine launches

T1566.002.definition: A targeted email with a link to a credential-phishing page or malware download.
T1566.002.attacker_use: steal logins or drop malware with a single click.
T1566.002.detection_hint: clicks on newly registered or lookalike domains arriving via mail; credentials posted to non-corporate login pages

T1566.004.definition: Phone-call phishing (vishing) — talking victims into granting access, often while posing as the IT helpdesk.
T1566.004.attacker_use: bypass technical controls entirely by exploiting people.
T1566.004.detection_hint: helpdesk-driven password or MFA resets followed by logons from new devices or locations (telemetry is limited — pair with helpdesk verification procedures)

T1567.002.definition: Uploading stolen data to cloud storage the attacker controls (Mega, S3 buckets, file-sharing sites).
T1567.002.attacker_use: hide the theft inside ordinary-looking cloud traffic.
T1567.002.detection_hint: large uploads to personal or rare cloud-storage domains; rclone or similar sync tools appearing on servers

T1573.definition: Encrypting the command-and-control channel so its content cannot be inspected.
T1573.attacker_use: keep their remote-control traffic unreadable to network monitoring.
T1573.detection_hint: encrypted traffic to rare destinations with odd or self-signed certificates; fixed-interval encrypted beacons

T1621.definition: Bombarding a user with MFA push prompts until they tap Approve — 'MFA fatigue'.
T1621.attacker_use: turn a stolen password into a full login by exhausting the victim's patience.
T1621.detection_hint: bursts of MFA denials or timeouts for one account followed by an approval, especially from a new location

T1685.definition: Turning off or reconfiguring your security tools — antivirus, EDR, or logging.
T1685.attacker_use: blind the defenses before the real attack starts.
T1685.detection_hint: security services stopped or exclusions added; security processes terminated; audit policy changes

T1685.005.definition: Wiping the Windows event logs to erase evidence of what was done.
T1685.005.attacker_use: cover their tracks after the fact.
T1685.005.detection_hint: wevtutil cl executions; Windows 'audit log was cleared' events (1102)
